transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-08
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Ivy Chen (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (BlueFjord Head of Search), Maya Singh (BlueFjord ML), Aaron Lee (BlueFjord Platform)

Summary: quick technical deep dive focused on embeddings/reranking perf and cost. Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted for a reranking pipeline, cares about latency SLOs (~50-150ms p95), cost at scale, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Action items were assigned.

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro. I'm lena from Redwood, this is marco and ivy on the se side. can you confirm attendees from bluefjord?
[00:12] Raj: yeah this is raj, maya, aaron here. thanks for running this. rough context — we have a search + rerank pipeline, embed then ANN retrieve then dense rerank with cross-encoder for top 50. Latency budget for user-facing rerank is tight, p95 ideally under 150ms end-to-end, p99 under 300ms for now.
[00:34] Marco: great. so we'll focus on two parts: embedding throughput/latency and the rerank stage. we'll talk batch sizing, vector dims, ANN vs brute-force, quantization, and how dedicated GPUs / private deploy affects network and overall latency.
[00:48] Maya: quick clarifier — when you say rerank stage do you mean the cross-encoder that scores pairs? that's the slow part for us. embeddings are used for retrieval and also for cheap rerank in some experiments.
[01:02] Ivy: yes exactly. many customers do a two-stage: fast retrieval via embeddings + ANN, then a cross-encoder on top N. downside is cross-encoder cost; we optimize by reducing candidate N and using batching/pipelining.

[05:15] [Marco] okay starting with embeddings: vector dims you mentioned — what are you currently using?
[05:21] Raj: we started with 512 dims from our encoder. trying 256 for perf but worry about loss in quality on tail queries.
[05:28] Marco: right. quick rules of thumb: 128/256 good for coarse retrieval, 512/768 better recall for narrow domains. higher dims increase memory and index size linearly, and increase compute for distance ops. For GPU inference, embedding compute time scales with dim but is also kernel-optimized.
[05:45] Maya: what about quantization for embeddings? we've seen papers about 8-bit quantization for vectors.
[05:52] Ivy: for embeddings you can quantize indexes (PQ, OPQ, IVF-PQ) without changing model outputs; that's ANN index quantization. For model-side quantization (INT8), embedding quality sometimes drops slightly but often acceptable if you retrain calibration. we recommend FP16 on GPU for embedding generation; INT8 permutations are experimental and need eval sets.
[06:10] Raj: ok got it. can you give ballpark latencies for embedding generation per query? we run both online single-query and batched bulk embed jobs.
[06:20] Marco: on a modern A10/A100-like GPU: single-query FP16 embedding at 512 dims is roughly 4-8ms on GPU depending on model; CPU can be 30-120ms. Batch throughput improves amortized cost — e.g., batch size 32 can get per-sample latency down to ~1-2ms on GPU. But beware batching increases tail latency if you wait to fill a batch.
[06:45] Aaron: what's our expected qps? we estimate 400 qps peak for embeds during traffic spikes (not all are rerank).
[06:52] Ivy: for 400 qps you likely want dedicated capacity or autoscaled fleet with warm pools. for Hosted we can guarantee throughput tiers but for predictable p99 you might prefer Dedicated to avoid cold start variability.

[10:00] [Lena] moving to retrieval and rerank: assume retrieval gives top 200 candidates, then you run a reranker on top 50. what's the typical breakdown in time?
[10:12] Marco: retrieval with ANN (FAISS HNSW) on CPU is sub-10ms for 50-100ms index sizes depending on index and memory locality; GPU-accelerated retrieval also available for dense indexes. Reranker — a cross-encoder 6-8B model on GPU FP16 may cost ~10-30ms per pair, so for 50 pairs that's 500-1500ms if running sequentially. So batching/pooling and model selection matter a lot.
[10:45] Maya: that seems high. how do other customers keep end-to-end sub-200ms?
[10:51] Marco: common patterns: reduce candidate N (e.g., 10-20) with stronger retrieval, use a smaller cross-encoder for latency-sensitive paths, or use a lightweight reranker that scores pairs in a vectorized fashion (siamese models). Another is cascade: lightweight filter then expensive rerank on smaller subset, and run reranker asynchronously for non-blocking parts.

[15:30] [Aaron] can you explain KV cache mentions? i thought KV cache is for autoregressive models — how does it help here?
[15:38] Ivy: good point. KV cache is largely for decoder-based autoregressive generation; for reranking it's less relevant. we mentioned KV cache earlier because some pipelines mix generation with reranking (e.g., generate candidate answers then rerank). for pure embeddings/rerank, caching at feature level (cached embeddings for frequently seen docs) and result caching for top-K queries matters more. prefix caching and k-v style caches are useful in hybrid pipelines.
[16:10] Raj: so we should focus on embedding cache and ANN warm caches rather than kv cache.
[16:15] Marco: yes. warm ANN index in-memory on Dedicated nodes, pre-warm cache after deploys to avoid cold p99 spikes. Also serving runtime supports prefetching and async index load.

[20:05] [Marco] quantization tradeoffs — concrete numbers: FP16 for model gives near-identical quality and 2x memory savings vs FP32. INT8 can give ~2-4x memory and speedups on some kernels but may induce 1-3% recall degradation depending on model and task. For embedding indexes, PQ/OPQ often drops recall if you use very aggressive compression; test on representational queries.
[20:35] Maya: we care about top-of-funnel recall more than micro-ndcg, but tail queries matter for enterprise. can you quantify impact for 512->256 dims?
[20:44] Marco: typical hit-rate drop from 512->256 is modest for generic corpora (a few percentage points) but for specialized domains it can be larger. we recommend A/B eval on holdout set. our SE will run bench with dims 128/256/512 using your query logs to show tradeoffs.

[25:00] [Ivy] batching strategies — number one rule: don't batch at the expense of violating p95 SLO. for embedding gen, use small micro-batches (4-16) with adaptive batching (lower latency when qps low, grow batch size when qps high). For rerank cross-encoder, vectorized scoring of pairs across the batch is key: pack pairs into batches so GPU utilization is high. use our runtime's continuous batching to reduce tail latency while improving throughput.
[25:50] Raj: continuous batching? can you describe how that works?
[25:56] Marco: it's an adaptive batching scheduler — it will flush batches on timeout threshold (e.g., 10ms) or when size target reached. so if requests are sporadic you won't wait 100ms to fill a batch. you can tune timeouts per route.

[30:10] [Marco] networking / VPC implications: if you use Private (VPC) deployment, keep cross-az network hop low. we typically recommend colocating index and model serving in same subnet to avoid egress latency. for Hosted, there is minimal egress overhead but for on-prem you need to account for internal network. encryption at rest/in transit can add a few ms due to TLS.
[30:42] Aaron: what about model sharding and KV memory footprint for large indexes?
[30:48] Ivy: index sharding is common; FAISS supports sharding—each shard held in-memory on separate nodes. model shard for giant cross-encoders is a different problem — for 7B+ models you need multi-GPU and that adds interconnect latency (NCCL). For rerank where latency matters, we often recommend smaller single-GPU models rather than sharded large models.

[35:00] [Maya] cost discussion: interested in unit economics — how do batch size and dims affect cost per query?
[35:10] Marco: rough example: GPU hourly cost amortized to per-query depends on qps and utilization. if you can batch to 64 you might get cost per embed down by 4-10x vs single-query CPU. dims increase memory and slightly compute; doubling dims roughly doubles raw compute for distance ops and embedding generation. Using Dedicated reserved slots reduces $/token or $/embed compared to on-demand hosted. We'll provide TCO scenarios in the pricing sheet.

[40:20] [Ivy] benchmarks we propose: run embedding generation on A10/A100 equivalent, dims 128/256/512, batch sizes [1,4,16,32,64]. measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput. For reranker, benchmark cross-encoder small/med models (e.g., distilled bi-encoder vs 2B cross-encoder) on single GPU with pair batchings of [8,16,32]. We'll run 10k representative queries provided by Raj.

[45:00] Raj: ok we'll provide scrubbed logs — about 1k sample now, can share 10k after legal clearance.
[45:10] Lena: thanks — we'll treat data carefully and redact PII.

[48:30] [Marco] pitfalls/observed gotchas: 1) don't over-quantize index without eval; 2) cold-start of index or model causes p99 spikes — pre-warm; 3) batching timeouts misconfigured will either inflate latency or lower throughput; 4) network egress for private deployments sometimes forgotten in SLOs.

[52:00] Aaron: if we go private/on-prem what's the deployment path? we need KMS/HSM integration and SOC2 audit reports.
[52:12] Ivy: Private deployment options: a VPC-enabled control plane with customer-managed data plane in their cloud, or fully on-prem bundle. KMS integration is supported via customer-managed keys (we have docs). SOC2 and ISO docs will be shared. for on-prem orchestration we provide helm charts and runtime bundles that work with Kubernetes; we recommend Dedicated for initial pilot.

[57:00] [Lena] recap: Marco will run benchmarks (dims & batching) using Raj's logs; Ivy will prepare index/quantization config and security checklist; I will send pricing and next steps. target dates as agreed.
[57:30] Raj: thanks all looks actionable — main risk is cross-encoder cost; we'll evaluate smaller models vs more aggressive retrieval.
[58:05] Maya: quick Q: do you have example FAISS indexes for 100M vectors?
[58:12] Marco: yes we'll share config files and memory sizing; for 100M at 512 dims expect tens to low hundreds of GB depending on PQ compression. we'll include concrete numbers in the artifact link.
[59:00] [Lena] links mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (will share), FAISS config gist, security docs.
[61:00] [Lena] closing — thanks everyone, we'll follow up in calendar.

End transcript.
